Wave
wāv
n. (a swell or billow of water; rendering Hebrew gal, mishbar, Greek kuma, kludōn)
Saxon wafian, to fluctuate. Scripture's waves are the standing figure for instability — in the sea, in the doubter, and in the false teacher.

Biblical Definition

A wave in Scripture is motion without direction, and it becomes the Bible's picture of three things. Of affliction: “Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me” (Psa 42:7) — and note the possessive, thy waves; the psalmist assigns his floods to God rather than to chance, which is the only reason he can go on to hope in Him. Of danger: “there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full” (Mar 4:37). Of the divided mind: “let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed” (Jas 1:6) — a man who prays while reserving judgment is not asking, he is drifting. And of the false teacher, in Jude's brutal image: “Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame” (Jud 1:13). The sea is loud, impressive, restless, and it produces nothing but foam. So does a ministry without truth.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines wave as a moving swell or volume of water, a billow; and to waver as to fluctuate, to be unsettled in opinion.

expand to see more

WAVE, n. A moving swell or volume of water; usually, a swell raised and driven by wind.

2. Unevenness; inequality of surface.

3. The line or streak of luster on cloth watered and calendered.

WAVER, v.i. To play or move to and fro; to fluctuate; to be unsettled in opinion.

Key Scripture

Psa 42:7 — "Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me."

Mar 4:37 — "And there arose a great storm of wind, and the waves beat into the ship, so that it was now full."

Jas 1:6 — "But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed."

Jud 1:13 — "Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever."

Modern Corruption

Doubt has been promoted from an ailment to a virtue — the honest posture of a thoughtful faith — where James calls the wavering man unstable in all his ways and tells him not to expect an answer.

expand to see more

A large body of contemporary religious writing treats settled conviction as arrogance and perpetual questioning as maturity, so that the man James describes as a wave driven and tossed is recast as the model believer. James is blunt in the other direction: let him not think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord. This is not a rebuke of the man who brings real perplexity to God — the psalms are full of that, and Psalm 42 is one of them. It is a rebuke of asking while withholding trust, praying with one hand and hedging with the other.

The distinction is visible in Psalm 42 itself. The psalmist is overwhelmed, and he says so; but he calls the billows thine, and he preaches to his own soul to hope in God. That is faith under water, not wavering. Jude then shows where cultivated instability ends when it takes up a pulpit: raging waves foaming out their own shame — noise, motion, and nothing left on the sand.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew gal (H1530), a heap or wave, and mishbar (H4867), a breaker; Greek kuma (G2949), a wave, and kludōn (G2830), a surge — instability in the sea and in the soul.

expand to see more

Hebrew gal (H1530) — a wave, billow, heap; “all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me” (Psa 42:7).

Greek kuma (G2949) — a wave, billow; the waves beating into the ship (Mar 4:37) and the raging waves of Jud 1:13.

Greek kludōn (G2830) — a surge or tossing; the wave of the sea driven with the wind (Jas 1:6).

Usage

"“All thy waves and thy billows are gone over me” — the floods assigned to God, not to chance."

"“He that wavereth is like a wave of the sea” — motion mistaken for honesty."

"“Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame” — the false teacher, described."
